# Evaluating an agent

`replaylab-eval` plays a language model through exactly the campaign a scripted
policy plays: the same pools, the same hidden outcomes and the same scoring. The
only difference is that each batch comes from a model reasoning with the tools it
was given. Install the extras first with `uv sync --extra eval`.

## The pieces

**Conditions** are the arms of an experiment, defined in
`config/conditions.yaml` as an `include` list (tool groups or tool names) and an
optional `exclude` list. Every condition receives the *same* system prompt; only
the tool set changes, so comparing two conditions measures exactly that
difference. To print the resolved tool list of each condition:

```bash
replaylab-eval conditions
```

**Models and prices** live in `config/models.yaml` and `config/prices.yaml`, one
entry per model key. The API key is read from the environment variable named in
the config, never from the repository. Prices feed the spend guard, so a model
without a price cannot run.

**One records file per experiment.** Each finished episode appends one JSON line
to `<run-dir>/episodes.jsonl`. The line holds the outcome (`scores`), the full
conversation (`messages`), a per-call audit (`tool_calls`), token usage and cost,
the stop reason, quality `flags`, and the `config_hash` and `git_sha` that
produced it. An episode that fails (provider error, truncated reply, spending
cap) writes **no line at all**, so rerunning the same command plays exactly the
missing episodes and skips the recorded ones.

## The workflow

```bash
# 1. pilot: play a few episodes, measure their cost, project the whole matrix
replaylab-eval pilot --run-dir runs/x --model deepseek \
    --games N-dev --conditions A,B1 --trials 20 --max-usd 1

# 2. run: play every missing episode of the matrix (resumable)
replaylab-eval run --run-dir runs/x --model deepseek \
    --games N-dev --conditions A,B1 --trials 20 --max-usd 1

# 3. baselines on the same seeds, in the same records file
replaylab-eval scripted --run-dir runs/x --games N-dev \
    --policies random,learner,learner_sim,learner_sim_purchased --trials 20

# 4. paired comparison: a minus b, bootstrapped over seeds
replaylab-eval compare --records runs/x/episodes.jsonl \
    --game N-dev --a B1 --b scripted:learner_sim --ci 0.9

# 5. read the whole run as one page
replaylab-eval view --run-dir runs/x
```

`pilot` and `run` both refuse to start when the projected cost exceeds
`--max-usd`. Once a run has started, the cap is checked before **every** model
call, and the running total is saved in `spend.json`, so a resumed run counts
against the same cap. Caps are cumulative per run directory: to extend an
experiment, raise the cap to cover what has been spent plus the new projection.

## Why the comparisons are fair

* **Pairing.** An episode's seed depends only on `(game, trial)`, never on the
  condition or the model, so `B1` and `scripted:learner_sim` face the same pool
  order and the same aliases. `compare` refuses to run unless both sides cover
  exactly the same seeds. It reports the mean paired difference, a bootstrap
  interval and the win/tie/loss count; `--trial-range` restricts it to a block of
  trials.
* **One configuration per claim.** `config_hash` covers the model, prices,
  prompts, conditions, tool descriptions and limits, so two records with the
  same hash come from the same configuration. The git commit is stored next to
  it.
* **No replaying for luck.** A recorded episode is never deleted or played again.
  A *failed* episode is replayed, because it was never recorded as data.

## Reading a run

`compare` prints one JSON object: `mean_diff` (a − b; positive means a did
better), `ci_low` and `ci_high`, `wins`, `ties`, `losses` and `n`. Before reading
any hit counts, check the run's health as the reports do: few or no failure
lines in `errors.jsonl`, every episode ending `finished` or `agent_stopped`, a
single `config_hash`, and every scripted row present for the trials being judged.
Then read a couple of transcripts in the viewer, which shows the `flags` totals
next to every verdict.

The viewer (`replaylab-eval view`) turns a records file into one self-contained
HTML page: each episode's tool timeline, the hidden pool under its aliases, and,
optionally, scripted episodes overlaid as ghosts. Scripted play is deterministic
for a given seed, so the overlay is exact. Because the page reveals outcomes the
agent never bought, it is for people only and must never be shown to a model.

When a campaign ends, the model is asked once more, **without tools**, for the
plain-text summary the system prompt promises; it appears as the last message in
the viewer. This step is best effort: if the provider fails, the finished
episode is still recorded and flagged `closing_summary_failed`.

## Before believing an experiment

A comparison is only as good as the discipline behind it. Decide the question,
the trials and the pass/fail rule *before* running; check validity before
reading outcomes; and report every comparison that was planned, not only the
flattering ones. The project's working notes record each registration and its
result in that order.
